lines.text: My letter reached Greyhollow on the night I went under the cathedral. I had written it the night after Wren's arrow, when everything still seemed possible.
Tobin told me later that Bram read it aloud in the hall, standing up, like a proclamation.
To Bram, and everyone. Wren has beaten the King's own archer. The Lowmarket carried her on their shoulders, and she let them.
The hall went wild. Granny banged her axe on the table. Garrow pretended he wasn't crying, and failed.
Oswin is sober and frightening. Tamsin is clever. Ilse says the pups are not, under any circumstances, to be let into the bathhouse.
The pups were in the bathhouse at that very moment. Nobody said a word.
Then my wards insisted on reading the rest themselves, all at once, the way they did everything.
I. Have. Fixed. An. Aqueduct. What's an aqueduct?
A river with legs.
Does it say anything about me? Does it? Does it say Tilda?
It didn't. Bram read a line about her anyway, made up on the spot. It was the best line in the letter.
Tell Tilda she is the bravest girl in Greyhollow, and that Ash misses her terribly.
The last line was the only one I had written slowly.
Say hello to the lamp for me. I'll be home before midwinter.
By the time they read it, Wren had lost, Oswin was burned, Ilse was in a cell, and I was under the cathedral. Every line was wrong except the last. I meant the last one.
Then Kell came in from the night with snow in his braids, and the hall went quiet.
The riders are back, Steward. Twelve this time. They are walking the walls in the dark with knotted ropes. Measuring.
Bram went up on the wall. Out in the snow, little lanterns crept along its foot, stopping and starting.
Scouts count men. These are counting stones. You only count a wall's stones if you mean to bring ladders.
He sent riders to Kesting and Marrick, lit the beacon to Saltmouth, and wrote to me. Two lines, this time. I never got them.
Late that night, my wards couldn't sleep. They asked Bram for my song. The one I never learned.
Bram had not sung it in fifteen years. He sang it then, slow and low, like wind going round a chimney.
And far to the south, deep under the Cathedral of the Seven, someone else was humming it too.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter one hundred and two, coming soon.
